modelNote:
Wardley Map of Bicycle Production: value chain from rider need through frame, drivetrain, and wheelset down to raw materials, contract manufacturing, and global logistics.

Converted from wardley-bicycle-production.json by wardley-chat-to-rcn.js on 2026-08-11.

Source axis: commodity-right. Stored in RCN convention — evolution 0=Genesis to 1=Commodity, visibility 1=visible.

nodes.label: Rideable Bicycle
nodes.note: The user's need: a working, fit-for-purpose bicycle for commuting, sport, or leisure. The category is fully commodity — bikes are ubiquitous and buyers expect them to work out of the box. Sits at the visibility ceiling because everything below serves this outcome.

nodes.label: Retail and Fulfillment
nodes.note: Bricks-and-mortar bike shops still dominate service and fit, but direct-to-consumer brands (Canyon, YT, Commencal) have taken roughly 15% of premium sales shipping in a box. Productized: several viable channel models coexist. Pushed toward commodity by Amazon-style logistics and by the post-2022 inventory glut forcing brand discounting.

nodes.label: Brand and Model Design
nodes.note: The naming, geometry, positioning, and paint that turn a generic frame into a Specialized Tarmac or a Surly Cross-Check. Firmly in Product; dozens of brands survive by owning a category niche. Pinned by consumer preference for identity and by dealer network economics.

nodes.label: Frameset
nodes.note: The component that most defines ride character and price. Aluminum framesets are near-commodity, carbon is Product with real differentiation in layup and mould, steel spans custom builders to bulk imports. Held back from commodity by proprietary integration — internal cabling, brand-specific seatposts, headset standards.

nodes.label: Drivetrain
nodes.note: Shimano holds roughly half the global market, SRAM and Campagnolo split most of the rest, and the chainline, cassette, and brake interfaces are effectively industry-wide. Deep Product sliding into Commodity — Shimano's 12-speed Hyperglide+ is spec'd across price tiers from budget to pro. Pinned by the cost of building a competing drivetrain and by compatibility lock-in of installed chainrings and shifters.

nodes.label: Wheelset
nodes.note: Machine-built wheels from DT Swiss, Shimano, and Chinese OEMs cover the OEM market at commodity prices; hand-built and premium carbon wheels remain Product with real differentiation. Pushed rightward by robotic lacing and by direct-from-factory carbon wheels sold online. Pinned by hub patents (DT Swiss ratchet, Industry Nine) and by the tacit skill of wheelbuilding at the top.

nodes.label: Brake System
nodes.note: Hydraulic disc has displaced rim brakes across almost every category above entry-level in a decade. Late Product moving toward Commodity as SRAM, Shimano, Tektro, and TRP all field competent hydraulic systems. Pinned briefly by mounting-standard fragmentation (flat mount, post mount), which is eroding.

nodes.label: E-bike Powertrain
nodes.note: Motor, battery, controller, and display treated as one purchase decision. Bosch owns roughly half the mid-drive market in Europe; Shimano EP8 and Yamaha PW are the main rivals; Bafang serves the commodity end. Sits at the Custom/Product boundary because motor placement, torque curves, and battery integration still vary. Pulled toward Product by EN 15194 and by consumer expectation of app-based diagnostics.

nodes.label: Frame Assembly Contract Manufacturing
nodes.note: Giant Manufacturing and Merida in Taiwan, plus a dozen mainland Chinese factories, assemble the majority of the world's mid- and high-end bicycles. Deep Commodity in that any brand can source competent assembly on standard terms; short of pure utility because carbon layup quality and QC discipline still vary between factories. Being reshaped by tariff-driven relocation to Vietnam and Cambodia.

nodes.label: Carbon Fiber Layup
nodes.note: The skilled hand-layup and autoclave curing that turns Toray prepreg into a frame or rim. Product because layup schedules, ply orientation, and mould design remain proprietary and quality-variable. Chinese factories have closed most of the gap on execution but not on engineering IP. Pulled toward commodity by open-mould frames sold under private label; pinned by liability exposure and by brands' incentive to protect layup as a moat.

nodes.label: Tires and Rubber Compounds
nodes.note: Continental, Maxxis, Schwalbe, Vittoria, and Michelin lead a productized market where tread pattern, casing TPI, and rubber compound genuinely differ. Late Product: tubeless-ready is the OEM default, hookless rim compatibility is standardizing, Chinese manufacturers are producing credible copies. Pinned by rolling-resistance testing and by the fact that riders feel a bad tire immediately.

nodes.label: Aluminum and Steel Tubing
nodes.note: Alloy tubing (6061, 7005) and steel tubing (chromoly, high-tensile) are commodity metals sold by weight. Reynolds and Columbus survive as premium brands mainly through heat-treatment and butting IP, but the base material is a global commodity. Pinned by decades of standardized diameters and by the fact that most frame factories can hydroform or butt tubing in-house.

nodes.label: Bearings and Fasteners
nodes.note: Sealed cartridge bearings (6902, 6802) and standard metric fasteners, sourced by the crate from generalist suppliers. Pure utility. Enve and Chris King charge a premium for tighter tolerances, but the commodity market sets the floor.

nodes.label: Global Container Shipping
nodes.note: 40-foot containers moving from Kaohsiung and Shenzhen to Los Angeles, Rotterdam, and Felixstowe. Pure commodity utility — Maersk, MSC, and Cosco compete on price and schedule. The 2021-2022 rate spike briefly turned this layer into a product decision when some brands chartered vessels, but cadence has normalized.
